OIIX.name: FIR Tehran
OIIX.conflictType: Interstate conflict — Iran vs Israel/US (fragile ceasefire)
OIIX.narrative: EASA's CZIB-2026-04 reflects a ceasefire that has held since April 2026 but remains fragile, with an elevated Iranian air-defence posture that raises the risk of civil aircraft being misidentified. EASA has warned escalation could resume with little notice. The eastern part of the FIR was partially reopened for overflights in June 2026, while the western part remains closed; some overflights above FL285 are possible via specific temporary routes linking Oman/UAE with Central Asia, the Caucasus and Turkey. Several radar systems remain degraded and many western airports are still closed or daytime-only. The shoot-down of Ukraine International Airlines flight 752 over Tehran in January 2020 illustrates how quickly the situation can deteriorate. Iran has previously conducted missile activity close to busy international routes with little warning to civil aviation. Key timeline: March 2026 — FIR closed following large-scale US and Israeli strikes on Iranian military targets and subsequent Iranian missile and drone retaliation. June 2026 — eastern portion partially reopened. July 2026 — EASA's current CZIB continues to advise operators not to operate at any altitude; the US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Most Europe-Asia traffic continues to route south via Egypt/Saudi or north via the Caucasus/Afghanistan.

cross.detail: Some overflights above FL285 are possible via specific temporary routes, but western Iran remains heavily restricted. Several radar systems remain degraded, many western airports are still closed or daytime-only, and most operators continue avoiding the airspace.

Consistent with narrative. Additional context: several states continue to warn against operations in Iranian airspace. Earlier milestones — June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes; October 2024: mutual missile attacks led most operators to avoid both airspaces; January 2020: UIA752 shoot-down over Tehran.

ORBB.name: FIR Baghdad
ORBB.conflictType: Non-state armed groups (IBMGs) + Iranian missile/drone spillover
ORBB.narrative: Despite the regional ceasefire, EASA cites recurrent Iranian drone and ballistic-missile strikes reaching Iraqi airspace, alongside the continued presence of Iranian-backed militant groups (IBMGs), as reasons the Baghdad FIR remains a do-not-operate zone. The FIR reopened to overflights in June 2026 following the US-Iran ceasefire, with north-south routes available, but most Europe-Asia traffic still routes south via Egypt/Saudi or north via the Caucasus/Afghanistan. Primary risks include missile and drone activity linked to regional conflicts, misidentification by air-defence systems operated by both local and foreign military forces, and an ongoing threat from terrorist groups with portable anti-aircraft weaponry. Key timeline: April 2023 — drone and missile attacks in northern Iraq from Turkey and Iran, including strikes near ORSU and ORER. April 2024 — FIR closed due to Iranian drone and missile strike on Israel. June 2025 — airspace closed following Israeli missile attack on Iran, with missiles and drones transiting Iraqi airspace. March 2026 — FIR closed following US and Israeli strikes on Iran and subsequent retaliation. June 2026 — FIR reopened to overflights. July 2026 — EASA's current CZIB continues to advise operators not to operate at any altitude.

cross.detail: Iraq is open for overflights again, but western Iran's continued restrictions mean the old Europe-Asia corridor has not returned. Some airlines are using Iraq, but main flows remain north via the Caucasus/Afghanistan or south via Egypt/Saudi/Oman.
Consistent with narrative. Additional context: October 2021 — US operators permitted to overfly the ORBB/Baghdad FIR above FL320 under updated FAA restrictions.

OLBB.name: FIR Beirut
OLBB.narrative: A Trilateral Framework Agreement between Israel, Lebanon and the US (26 June 2026) is a step toward consolidating the ceasefire, but EASA notes its long-term implementation is uncertain, and that Lebanon has not shown it can proactively manage airspace risk. Israeli airstrikes in Lebanon have continued despite repeated ceasefire extensions and diplomatic efforts (February–July 2026). Primary risks are military activity linked to the Israel-Hezbollah conflict and the wider regional security situation, including missile and drone activity. Some states allow limited operations to OLBA/Beirut provided arrivals and departures remain over the Mediterranean Sea. GNSS spoofing and jamming have been reported in the FIR from November 2023 onwards. July 2026 — EASA's current CZIB continues to advise operators not to operate at any altitude.

cross.detail: Consistent with narrative. Additional context: October 2024 — Israel launched a ground operation against Hezbollah in southern Lebanon. Several states maintain long-standing warnings advising operators to avoid Lebanese airspace.

OJAC.name: FIR Amman
OJAC.conflictType: Missile/drone overflight risk (regional spillover, no direct conflict on Jordanian soil)
OJAC.narrative: Jordan's airspace has repeatedly seen Iranian missiles and drones pass through en route to other targets, intercepted by Jordanian and allied air defences. Jordanian authorities have not published any airspace restrictions of their own despite this activity. The FIR remains open and operating normally through the current escalation, though it is not a major transit route for Europe-Asia traffic, with most operators continuing to route via Egypt and Saudi Arabia. EASA issued an Information Note in July 2026 advising operators to take the potential risk into account before operating in the FIR. Key events: October 2023 — Jordan intercepted drones and missiles during regional escalation. April 2024 — Jordan temporarily closed its airspace during the Iranian drone and missile attack on Israel. February–July 2026 — Jordan remained open throughout the Iran conflict, although missile and drone activity affected several neighbouring countries.

cross.detail: Open and operating normally. In practice still not a major transit route for Europe-Asia traffic; most operators continue to route via Egypt and Saudi Arabia.

Consistent with narrative. Additional context: EASA's current Information Note advises operators to take the potential risk into account before operating in the OJAC/Amman FIR. No significant downgrades to recent airspace warnings.

OKAC.name: FIR Kuwait
OKAC.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OKAC.narrative: Kuwait hosts major US military facilities, making it a plausible target for Iranian retaliation and increasing the risk of civil aircraft being caught up in an attack or an air-defence response. The FIR remains open for arrivals and departures only — overflights continue to be prohibited, with prior approval required for flights to or from OKKK/Kuwait. Restrictions are extended until at least 4 August 2026. Missile and drone strikes damaged OKKK/Kuwait airport in March 2026. The FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict before settling at arrivals/departures-only status. EASA now advises operators not to operate at any altitude under its current CZIB.

cross.detail: Airspace restrictions extended until at least 4 August. Overflights remain prohibited; only arrivals to and departures from OKKK/Kuwait are permitted, with prior approval.
Consistent with narrative. Additional context: June 2025 — Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes across the region. No significant downgrades to recent airspace warnings.

OBBB.name: FIR Bahrain
OBBB.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OBBB.narrative: As with Kuwait and Qatar, the US military presence in Bahrain is the main driver of EASA's risk assessment for this FIR. Bahrain lies close to several key military facilities in the Gulf region. The FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict before reopening to normal overflight operations. Iranian missile and drone attacks in March 2026 targeted several Gulf states, including incidents affecting airspace around Bahrain. EASA now advises operators not to operate at any altitude under its current CZIB, even though the FIR is currently open to overflights. Note that nearby airspace — especially Kuwait — remains restricted and can affect routing.

cross.detail: Bahrain is open to overflights again. Nearby airspace, especially Kuwait, remains restricted and can affect routing. EASA advises operators to avoid the FIR at all levels.

Consistent with narrative. Additional context: June 2025 — Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings across the region. No significant downgrades to recent airspace warnings.

OTDF.name: FIR Doha
OTDF.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OTDF.narrative: Qatar hosts significant US forces and has itself been targeted by Iranian strikes during the recent escalation, keeping it on EASA's do-not-operate list even as operational conditions ease. The FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict before reopening to largely normal overflight operations. An Iranian missile strike was reported at Al Udeid Air Base near Doha in March 2026. Earlier temporary restricted areas and arrival/departure route-segment restrictions have been withdrawn, though some temporary restricted areas and military activity remain. EASA now advises operators not to operate at any altitude under its current CZIB.

cross.detail: Qatar has reopened to overflights; earlier restrictions on waypoints and arrival/departure route segments have been withdrawn, though some temporary restricted areas and military activity remain. EASA now advises operators to avoid the FIR at all levels.

Consistent with narrative. Additional context: June 2025 — Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings across the region. No significant downgrades to recent airspace warnings.

OMAE.name: FIR Emirates
OMAE.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OMAE.narrative: The UAE's proximity to the Strait of Hormuz and its role as a regional hub keep it firmly within EASA's risk assessment, despite being operationally busy. The FIR remains open to overflights, with traffic managed through a mix of normal ATS routes and temporary RNAV corridors. GPS interference continues to be one of the most significant operational issues across the FIR. EASA advises operators not to operate at any altitude under its current CZIB.

cross.detail: UAE remains open to overflights via normal ATS routes and temporary RNAV corridors. GPS interference continues to be one of the biggest operational issues across the FIR. EASA advises operators to avoid the FIR at all levels.

OOMM.name: FIR Muscat — west of 58°E only
OOMM.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OOMM.narrative: Unlike other Gulf FIRs, only the western portion of Omani/Gulf of Oman waters is covered — reflecting where commercial vessel attacks and Strait of Hormuz tension actually concentrate. Oman remained open throughout the Iran conflict and has become a key part of the main southern bypass route, carrying significant Europe-Asia overflight traffic via the Egypt-Saudi-Oman routing. The FIR is open but part of a managed corridor system, with flow measures and ongoing GNSS interference reports. EASA's current CZIB advises operators not to operate over the waters of the Gulf of Oman within the OOMM/Muscat FIR west of 58°E.

cross.detail: Oman remains one of the most useful FIRs in the region for the southern bypass. Open, but part of the managed corridor system with flow measures and ongoing GNSS interference reports.

Consistent with narrative. Additional context: June 2025 — Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings across the Gulf region. October 2024 — mutual missile attacks between Israel and Iran led many operators to avoid airspace between the two countries.

OSTT.name: FIR Damascus
OSTT.narrative: EASA's longest-running Middle East bulletin (19 revisions since 2017) reflects a still-unresolved multi-actor conflict. Traffic patterns have shifted: OSTT quietly reopened to some regional carriers in early 2025 as an alternative to the more restricted Iran/Iraq corridor, even though most Western operators continue to avoid it. Primary risks are military activity linked to the conflict in Syria — including Israeli airstrikes targeting Iranian and Hezbollah-linked positions — and the potential for misidentification by air-defence systems. Several countries continue to prohibit or advise against operations in the FIR. Key timeline: September 2018 — Russian IL-20 shot down in error near the Syria-Cyprus FIR boundary. February 2020 — an A320 approaching Damascus diverted after being caught in crossfire during Israeli airstrikes. October 2023 — airstrikes damaged runways at OSDI/Damascus and OSAP/Aleppo airports. December 2024 — FIR temporarily closed following the fall of the Assad regime. March 2026 — FIR closed following US and Israeli strikes on Iran and subsequent regional retaliation. January–July 2026 — gradual increase in overflights as some regional operators use Syria as an alternative to Iran and Iraq routing.

cross.detail: Syria has quietly become part of the regional routing picture again after years of almost no international overflight traffic.

Consistent with narrative. Additional context: the US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. Syrian airspace remains high risk despite some regional operators resuming use of it.

OYSC.name: FIR Sana'a only
OYSC.conflictType: Civil war + interstate spillover (Red Sea attacks)
OYSC.narrative: This bulletin covers only the Sana'a FIR, not the whole of Yemen. The ongoing civil war and Houthi involvement in the wider regional conflict keep the risk assessment unchanged since 2017. Primary risks are intentional targeting by terrorist groups with access to sophisticated anti-aircraft weaponry, and civil aircraft being caught in high-intensity military operations involving explosive drones and missiles. Saudi and Israeli airstrikes can occur at any time, including in the capital Sana'a. Several countries prohibit aircraft from overflying any land portion of the FIR; US operators can use offshore routes UT702 and M999, while others permit flights on overwater portions. OYSN/Sanaa Airport has been closed since damage from Israeli airstrikes in December 2024 and May 2025. Key timeline: January 2024 — US and UK airstrikes against Houthi rebels in response to Red Sea missile and drone attacks. December 2024 onwards — OYSN/Sanaa Airport closed due to airstrike damage. July 2026 — Yemen's government struck the OYSN/Sanaa Airport runway to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing.

cross.detail: Consistent with narrative. Additional context: Saudi airspace to the north and Somali airspace to the south also have associated risks. Earlier milestones — April–October 2022: all-party ceasefire. 2018–2022: frequent Saudi airstrikes on Sana'a and other targets in retaliation for Houthi drone attacks. 2017: OYSN/Sanaa Airport badly damaged by coalition airstrikes. September 2023: Houthi drone attacks near the Yemen-Saudi border.

UUWV.name: FIR Moscow and others (west of 60°E)
UUWV.conflictType: Interstate war — Russian invasion of Ukraine (air-defence risk)
UUWV.narrative: Issued after the likely accidental shoot-down of Azerbaijan Airlines flight 8243 near Grozny in December 2024, this bulletin reflects the risk that Russian air-defence systems responding to Ukrainian strikes pose to civil aircraft, compounded by widespread GNSS interference. Drone attacks across Russia have been intensifying, with some reaching as far as Siberia; hundreds of drones have been shot down recently, including in areas around Moscow. Russian air-defence systems are using surface-to-air missiles capable of reaching all altitudes, so the risk applies at every level. Most disruptions occur at night, but daytime incidents are now common. Large parts of Russian airspace near the border with Ukraine remain restricted. Primary risk is unintended targeting of civil aircraft by military near the Russia-Ukraine border, including misidentification — as with MAS17 and UIA752. Key timeline: January 2024 — crash of a military transport near Belgorod, approximately 20 nm from the Ukrainian border; both sides accused each other of shooting it down. January 2025 — EASA issued a new CZIB recommending against flights in western Russia (west of 60°E) following the December 2024 shoot-down near URMG/Grozny. July 2023 onwards — increasing frequency of drone strikes on Moscow and surrounding region, forcing temporary airport closures.

cross.detail: Consistent with narrative. Additional context: Ukraine's airspace has remained fully closed to civil aviation since the Russian invasion in February 2022. Several countries prohibit their operators from using Russian airspace near the FIR boundaries with Ukraine. August 2023: private jet carrying Wagner chief Yevgeny Prigozhin crashed en route from Moscow to St Petersburg on 23 August, with speculation of a bomb onboard.

UKBV.name: All Ukrainian FIRs
UKBV.narrative: In force since the day of the invasion, this remains one of the clearest and most stable prohibitions in this dataset — Ukraine itself has closed its FIRs to civil traffic by NOTAM. Russia, Belarus and Moldova have closed large sections of their own airspace near FIR boundaries with Ukraine. All major countries that regularly issue airspace warnings (the US, UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy) have issued total flight bans for Ukraine. Primary risks are unintended targeting of civil aircraft by military, including misidentification (as with MAS17 and UIA752), and potential loss of Ukrainian ATC service at short notice (e.g. from a cyber-attack). Prior to February 2022, two areas of concern existed: the conflict in the far east of Ukraine (UKDV/Dnipro FIR) and the disputed ATC authority over Crimea (UKFV/URFV/Simferopol FIR).

cross.detail: Consistent with narrative. Additional context: several other countries have also issued flight bans for Ukraine beyond those listed. Secondary risk includes potential lack of Ukrainian ATC service at short notice due to cyber-attack or other unforeseeable non-normal operating environments.

HSSS.name: FIR Khartoum
HSSS.conflictType: Civil war — Sudan Armed Forces (SAF) vs Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
HSSS.narrative: The ongoing SAF–RSF civil war has put anti-aircraft artillery, MANPADS and SAM systems into play across the whole of Sudanese airspace, keeping the entire Khartoum FIR off-limits. HSSK/Khartoum airport is closed, with no NOTAMs being issued; a contingency plan with published overflight routes via HSPN/Port Sudan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and South Sudan is available. Air navigation services in South Sudan remain suspended above FL245. Primary risk is security on the ground for any unplanned diversions; there have been reports of passenger jets being targeted by gunfire at HSSK/Khartoum Airport throughout the conflict. Secondary risk is Sudan's proximity to South Sudan, which has poor ATC provision for overflights below FL245. Key timeline: October 2021 — military coup; HSSK/Khartoum airport closed for two days. April 2023 — military coup on 15 April; Sudan's airspace closed. October 2024 — foreign-registered cargo aircraft shot down by local militia over North Darfur. May 2025 — drone attack targeting critical infrastructure including HSPN/Port Sudan airport. November 2025 — Il-76 reportedly shot down by surface-to-air missile near Babanusa, southern Sudan.

cross.detail: Consistent with narrative. Additional context: several countries have issued airspace warnings advising operators not to enter Sudanese airspace due to risks from anti-aircraft weaponry and military activity. Be aware of other active warnings in airspace close to Sudan.

HLLL.name: FIR Tripoli
HLLL.narrative: Libya's two rival governments and various non-state armed actors create a real risk of misidentification when crossing between areas controlled by different authorities. The one carve-out is for coastal airport approaches made from over the sea. Primary risk is misidentification by Libyan air-defence systems, or by militia who have threatened to shoot down aircraft operating in western Libya including at HLLM/Tripoli Mitiga airport. Military activity has been reported over the high seas, either operating as OAT or not in contact with ATC. Reliable ATC services cannot be guaranteed; there have been regular ATS and radar outages across the FIR, and severe VHF limitations have required operators to communicate with Malta ATC for guidance. Risk remains high across Libya at all flight levels. Key timeline: 2014 — HLLT/Tripoli airport closed after clashes between rival militias; most flights since operate from HLLM/Mitiga. January 2020 — multiple airstrikes targeting HLLM/Mitiga airport. November 2019 — militia declared a no-fly zone around Tripoli, threatening to shoot down civil aircraft. June 2022 — failed militia attempt to seize Tripoli, resulting in armed clashes and suspension of flights at HLLM/Mitiga. August 2022 — militia air-defence forces claimed to have shot down a US drone near Benghazi. August 2023 — major evacuation of aircraft from Tripoli due to violent clashes and gunfire at Mitiga airport. July 2023 — Italy cancelled its 10-year ban on flights to/from Libya.
HLLL.restrictionLabel: Do not operate, except flights to coastal airports approached from the sea, subject to ATC contact and your own risk assessment

cross.detail: Consistent with narrative. Additional context: total flight ban for US operators; several other countries have warnings in place. A civil war has been ongoing since 2014 with armed clashes between various rival militia groups; some progress was made in October 2020 with the formation of a new government.

DRRR.name: Malian territory, especially the north-east
DRRR.conflictType: Insurgency — non-state armed groups active across the Sahel
DRRR.narrative: Non-state armed groups operating in Mali, particularly in the north-east, are assessed to have MANPADS and SAM missile capability, which is why the restriction is altitude-based rather than a total ban. The conflict has continued since 2012 and the security situation remains volatile. ATS in Mali is provided by the GOOO/Dakar and DRRR/Niamey FIRs, which maintain a long-standing restriction for overflights of Mali to published ATS routes at FL320 and above. The US advises caution at all levels due to ongoing fighting, expanding militant activity, and the presence of a state-run paramilitary force operating anti-aircraft systems, military aircraft, UAS and electronic warfare equipment. Primary risks include MANPADS and other surface-to-air weapons, indirect fire near airports, and the potential for misidentification or spillover from military activity — with low-level and airport-phase operations carrying the highest exposure. Several countries advise operations at or above FL250 or FL260 and avoiding GATB/Timbuktu, GAGO/Gao and GAKL/Kidal. Key timeline: January 2017 and November 2016 — vehicle bomb and rocket attacks at GAGO/Gao and GATB/Timbuktu airports. April 2018 — militants attacked UN bases near GATB/Timbuktu using indirect fire and vehicle bombs. August 2020 — military coup; all airports closed for two days (overflights unaffected). December 2023 — Germany prohibited operators below FL260 in northern Mali; commercial flights to GATB/Timbuktu cancelled after shelling near the airport; a military jet crashed near GAGO/Gao, possibly shot down. September 2024 — insurgents breached GABS/Bamako and set the presidential jet on fire; multiple attacks across the city and temporary airport closure. April 2026 — security situation escalated sharply; coordinated attacks nationwide on 25 April, with gunfire and explosions near GABS/Bamako; France issued a new airspace warning advising French operators not to operate to/from GABS or use it as an alternate.

cross.detail: Consistent with narrative. Additional context: more detailed routing information can be found in the relevant ASECNA AIP SUP.

HCSM.name: Somali airspace
HCSM.conflictType: Insurgency — Al-Shabaab and related terrorist groups
HCSM.narrative: Terrorist organisations operating in Somalia are assessed to have confirmed anti-aircraft weaponry, possibly including MANPADS, driving the same FL260 altitude floor as Mali. The central government has little control of major cities and ports, with ongoing attacks from extremist militants targeting civilians and aviation interests. The US prohibits flights across the HCSM/Mogadishu FIR below FL260, except for flights transiting the overwater portion to/from HDAM/Djibouti. Several other countries have issued airspace warnings advising against operating below FL260. From November 2025, Somaliland has required a PPR from its own CAA for all overflights, while Somalia has reaffirmed through an AIC that it controls the entire FIR — expect conflicting permit instructions near Hargeisa and northern Somalia. There is also a risk from unauthorised ATC units issuing conflicting climb/descent instructions on the same frequency as Mogadishu Control. Key timeline: May 2020 — EMB-120 shot down on approach to Bardale airstrip, accidentally, by Ethiopian forces; all six on board killed. May 2022 — Class A airspace implemented in the FIR above FL245. October 2022 — Somali government warned HCMM/Mogadishu airport may be targeted by militant groups. August 2023 — reports of uncontrolled combat helicopters flying at FL030 without position or routing reports. February 2024 — multiple crew reports of a 'fake controller' on frequency issuing conflicting instructions.

cross.detail: Consistent with narrative. Additional context: 2020 onwards — multiple instances of Al-Shabaab attacks on HCMM/Mogadishu and nearby targets, including a UN compound.

OPKR.name: Baluchistan province (partial)
OPKR.conflictType: Insurgency (violent non-state actors) + Kashmir territorial dispute
OPKR.narrative: Violent non-state actor (VNSA) groups with confirmed MANPADS operate in Baluchistan. The Kashmir dispute separately raises misidentification risk further north. In May 2025, four days of cross-border strikes and shelling between India and Pakistan occurred in the Kashmir region; a ceasefire announced on 10 May has largely held but remains fragile. In February 2026, cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated, though no new airspace closures were issued and commercial traffic continues to transit the OAKX/Kabul FIR via P500 and G500. In January 2024, Iran conducted missile and drone strikes against a militant group in western Pakistan. GPS spoofing has been reported in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area since December 2023. Current guidance generally advises remaining at or above FL260. Key prior event: February–August 2019 — Pakistan closed its airspace to overflights following major clashes with India in the Kashmir region, including airstrikes on both sides.

cross.detail: Consistent with narrative. Additional context: several states and EASA maintain altitude-based restrictions rather than full avoidance. Primary risks are anti-aviation weaponry including potential MANPADS below FL260, and inadvertent risk from military activity or misidentification in the Kashmir region.

OPLR.name: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province (partial)
OPLR.conflictType: Insurgency (violent non-state actors) + Kashmir territorial dispute
OPLR.narrative: Covers the north-western province, where the Kashmir dispute adds a misidentification risk on top of the VNSA activity common to both restricted Pakistani provinces. In May 2025, four days of cross-border strikes and shelling between India and Pakistan occurred in the Kashmir region; a ceasefire announced on 10 May has largely held but remains fragile. In February 2026, cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated, though no new airspace closures were issued. GPS spoofing has been reported in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area, particularly around OPLA/Lahore, since December 2023. Current guidance generally advises remaining at or above FL260.

cross.detail: Consistent with narrative. Same risk picture as OPKR/Karachi FIR: altitude-based restrictions rather than full avoidance; primary risks from potential MANPADS below FL260 and misidentification risk in the Kashmir region. February–August 2019: Pakistan closed its airspace to overflights following major clashes with India.

OAKX.name: FIR Kabul
OAKX.conflictType: Post-conflict security vacuum — extremist groups active, limited air traffic services
OAKX.narrative: Since the 2021 Taliban takeover, Afghanistan has had little to no functioning air traffic control. The Kabul FIR is Class G airspace: crews use published contingency routes and TIBA procedures rather than normal ATC clearances. Traffic through the FIR increased from March 2026 as flights used the northern bypass route around the closed Middle East corridor following US and Israeli strikes on Iran. Some countries restrict overflights to airways P500 and G500 in the far east of the FIR; others allow overflights across the entire airspace at and above FL320. Primary risk is surface-to-air fire targeting aircraft at low altitudes; additionally, there is no ATC service and an extreme threat to aircraft and crew safety on the ground. Key timeline: August 2021 — US and allied forces withdrew; OAKX became uncontrolled Class G airspace. February 2026 — cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; commercial traffic continued to transit via P500 and G500. March 2026 — traffic increased through the FIR as flights used the northern bypass.

cross.detail: OAKX/Kabul FIR remains Class G with no normal ATS service; crews must use published contingency routes with TIBA procedures. Armenia and Azerbaijan remain important parts of the northern bypass, with steady overflight demand.

Consistent with narrative. Additional context: some countries restrict overflights to airways P500 and G500 in the far east of the FIR only; others allow overflights across the entire airspace at and above FL320.

HAAA.name: FIR Addis Ababa, north of 8.5°N
HAAA.conflictType: Regional/border tension — assessed by EASA as medium risk
HAAA.narrative: This is an EASA Information Note, not a CZIB — meaning EASA's risk assessment group judged the risk here as medium rather than high. Full analytical detail is restricted to the CZ Hub. A peace deal agreed in early November 2022 ended the Tigray conflict, but airspace warnings remain in place in several states. Primary risk is large-scale ceasefire violations involving missiles or anti-aircraft weaponry that could endanger overflights — civil aircraft being mistaken for a military target or caught in crossfire. Key timeline: November 2020 — major escalation in Tigray; several airways near the conflict zone closed by Ethiopian and Sudanese CAAs; rockets targeted HABD/Bahir Dar and HAGN/Gondar airports and missiles fired into Eritrea targeting HHAS/Asmara. July 2021 — HAAA/Addis FIR NOTAM closed airspace below FL290 over Tigray after a military transport was reportedly shot down near Mekele. November 2021 — western countries issued airspace and travel warnings for the Tigray region. November 2022 — peace deal agreed; Ethiopian Airlines planned to resume flights to HAMK/Mekele. February 2024 — new fighting flare-up in the Amhara region, including air strikes.
HAAA.restrictionLabel: Caution only — factor into your own risk assessment and routing, below FL 260

cross.detail: Consistent with narrative. Additional context: September 2018 — Ethiopian ATC controllers went on strike; the ECAA and Ethiopian Airlines recruited retired and foreign controllers, some not fully qualified for Ethiopian airspace; Ethiopia denied a strike was occurring; strike ended 7 September.

VYYF.name: FIR Yangon, below FL260
VYYF.conflictType: Internal armed conflict — assessed by EASA as medium risk
VYYF.narrative: As with Ethiopia, this is a medium-risk Information Note rather than a do-not-operate CZIB. France's own national guidance goes slightly further operationally, setting a hard altitude floor. The security situation has deteriorated since the military coup of February 2021, with conflict and violence across many parts of the country involving air strikes and armed clashes. Several countries have issued airspace warnings at the lower flight levels due to the potential risk from military operations, surface-to-air fire and anti-aviation weaponry. GPS jamming has been reported on airway N895 and in the north of the FIR for overflights between China and Bangladesh airspace. Key timeline: February 2021 — military coup; ATC strike at end of February left overflights without ATC service. September 2022 — a Myanmar National Airlines passenger was reportedly shot as bullets passed through the fuselage of an ATR 72 on approach to VYLK/Loikaw. April 2023 — VYYY/Yangon temporarily closed following an attack with improvised artillery rounds. September 2023 — attacks on an airbase adjacent to VYNT/Naypyitaw airport using an improvised drone; intermittent GPS jamming on airway N895. January 2024 — armed group shot down a military helicopter in Kachin state, likely using MANPADS.
VYYF.restrictionLabel: Caution only — factor into your own risk assessment and routing, below FL 260

cross.detail: Consistent with narrative. Additional context: increasing strikes and mass protests by opposition activists since the coup, as well as clashes with militia and airstrikes on areas where militia are known to be active.
